University of Georgia · AMAML Lab · 2024–2025

Electric-Field-Assisted Carbon Nanofiber Alignment in Polymer Composites

Using AC dielectrophoresis to controllably align CNFs during composite fabrication, and a computer vision system to track alignment state in real time.

Role
Graduate Researcher
Field Strength
100 V/mm AC
Frequency
1 kHz
Alignment Time
< 60 seconds
Resistance Drop
97.6%

The Problem

Carbon nanofibers are exceptional electrical conductors, but only when aligned. In most composite fabrication processes, CNFs are randomly dispersed in the polymer matrix. Random orientation means individual fibers rarely contact one another, leaving the composite as an effective insulator despite containing highly conductive material.

The challenge: how do you align fibers that are micrometers in diameter, suspended in a viscous liquid, after the material has already been deposited? And how do you know when alignment is actually complete?

Requirements and Constraints

  • Alignment must occur after deposition, within the processing window before the polymer cures
  • The method must be scalable and repeatable across electrode geometries
  • Alignment quality must be measurable and quantifiable, not just visually assessed
  • Process parameters (field strength, frequency) must be optimized for alignment speed and quality

Approach: AC Dielectrophoresis

Dielectrophoresis (DEP) is the movement of polarizable particles in a non-uniform electric field. Under an AC field, CNFs experience a torque that tends to align them along field lines. The key insight: AC fields can drive alignment without net particle transport, which means fibers move into orientation without clumping at the electrodes.

Copper electrodes were patterned to create a uniform field region, and the CNF-doped dimethylformamide (DMF) suspension was deposited between them. A signal generator supplied the AC field at controlled voltage and frequency.

Computer Vision Pipeline for Alignment Tracking

Visual assessment of alignment is subjective and slow. To make the process measurable, I built a real-time computer vision pipeline that processes microscopy frames and outputs quantitative alignment metrics.

The pipeline computes two scores per frame:

  • Continuity score — measures how connected the fiber network is, detecting when fibers have bridged to form conductive pathways
  • Angle score — measures how consistently fibers are oriented along the field direction

These two scores together drive a three-state classifier: DISPERSED → ALIGNING → ALIGNED. The system outputs the current state and logs the timestamp of each transition.

Parameter Optimization

Field strength and frequency both affect alignment speed. Running experiments across 50, 75, and 100 V/mm at frequencies from 100 Hz to 10 kHz revealed a clear optimum: 100 V/mm at 1 kHz minimized alignment time across all trials. Below 500 Hz, electrophoretic drift competes with alignment. Above 10 kHz, the field reversal is too fast for fibers to respond.

Results

97.6%
reduction in electrical resistance (1.1 MΩ → 26.5 kΩ)
<60s
alignment time at optimal parameters
1 kHz
optimal AC frequency for alignment across all field strengths
3-state
real-time CV classifier tracking DISPERSED / ALIGNING / ALIGNED

The combination of a quantifiable alignment metric and a real-time state classifier means the process can be stopped precisely when alignment is complete, rather than running for an arbitrary fixed duration.

What I Learned

The most useful thing this project taught me wasn't the DEP physics, which is well-established. It was that measurement is the bottleneck in most experimental work. Before the CV pipeline existed, "alignment" was a judgment call. After it, alignment was a number. That shift changed how we designed experiments, how we reported results, and how reproducible the process became.

The frequency sweep also showed something non-obvious: the worst-performing condition (100 Hz, 100 V/mm) actually produced faster initial motion than the optimum, because electrophoretic drift moves fibers quickly, just not into aligned orientation. Learning to distinguish fast movement from useful movement shaped how I interpreted the data.

TE Connectivity · Bangalore · Summer 2023

FEA-Driven Design Validation for OEM Electrical Connector Assemblies

Applying finite element analysis to validate connector designs under mechanical and thermal loading during new product introduction, reducing design iteration cycles.

Role
Project Intern
Tool
ANSYS Workbench
Focus
Structural + Thermal
Outcome
25% NPI cycle reduction

The Problem

New product introduction for high-current electrical connectors involves repeated physical build-and-test cycles to validate that a design meets mechanical and thermal specifications. Each cycle requires prototype fabrication, test setup, and failure analysis — a process that is expensive and slow when iteration is needed late in the design phase.

The question was whether simulation could front-load this validation work, catching design issues before physical prototypes are built.

Approach

Using ANSYS Workbench, I built FEA models of OEM connector assemblies and ran structural and thermal analyses to simulate real operating conditions. The models captured:

  • Mechanical stress under mating force and vibration loading
  • Thermal distribution at rated current, to identify hot spots and contact resistance concerns
  • Deformation under combined loading relevant to the target OEM's installation environment

Simulation results were compared against design specifications and fed back to the design team before physical builds were ordered. In cases where the model predicted failure modes, the geometry was revised in the CAD model and re-simulated without cutting a prototype.

Results

25%
reduction in NPI cycle time through earlier design validation
Fewer
physical prototype iterations by catching failures in simulation first

What I Learned

The biggest constraint wasn't the simulation itself, it was model fidelity. Contact interfaces between connector pins and housing are difficult to model accurately without careful mesh refinement and contact settings, and over-constraining the model produced misleadingly optimistic results. Getting comfortable with mesh convergence studies and sensitivity checks was the skill that made the simulation outputs credible rather than just impressive-looking.

Subros Limited · Noida · 2022

Assembly Line Process Improvement for Automotive HVAC Compressors

Analyzing and restructuring the compressor assembly sequence to reduce cycle time, improve throughput, and lower defect rate using lean manufacturing methods.

Role
Industrial Intern
Method
Lean / Process Mapping
Efficiency Gain
~12%
Defect Reduction
~5%

The Problem

Subros manufactures HVAC compressor assemblies for major automotive OEMs. The compressor assembly line had accumulated process inefficiencies over time: workstation layouts that created unnecessary motion, assembly steps sequenced sub-optimally, and inspection points positioned after rather than before defect-generating operations.

Defects were being caught late, requiring rework that consumed capacity and slowed throughput.

Approach

I mapped the full assembly sequence using value stream analysis, timing each station and identifying where operators were waiting, moving unnecessarily, or performing operations out of optimal sequence. Key findings:

  • Two workstations had high variability in cycle time due to tooling reach issues, not operator inconsistency
  • Leak test was positioned after a labor-intensive assembly stage, meaning rework from leak failures discarded significant prior work
  • Component staging at several stations required operators to leave their primary workspace to retrieve parts

Recommendations included repositioning the leak test earlier in the sequence, redesigning component staging fixtures at the two high-variability stations, and rebalancing work content across stations to reduce idle time at bottlenecks.

Results

~12%
improvement in assembly line efficiency after workstation redesign
~5%
reduction in defect rate by repositioning inspection earlier

What I Learned

Process improvement work lives or dies on how well you observe before you recommend. The most impactful change, moving the leak test earlier, came from watching what happened downstream of a failed test, not from the process documentation. The documentation said the line ran at a certain cycle time. The floor showed something different. That gap between documented process and actual process is where most improvement opportunities hide.

About

I'm Romit Dhar, a mechanical engineering M.S. candidate at the University of Georgia working in the AMAML Lab under Professor Kenan Song. My research focuses on electric-field-assisted nanoparticle alignment and microfluidic additive manufacturing.

Before graduate school I studied mechanical engineering at VIT (Vellore Institute of Technology) and did internships at TE Connectivity in Bangalore, where I worked on FEA for electrical connector assemblies, and at Subros in Noida, where I worked on assembly line process improvement for automotive HVAC compressors.

I'm interested in roles at the intersection of materials, manufacturing process development, and simulation. I expect to complete my thesis and graduate in May 2027.

Research Interests

Composite materials, dielectrophoresis, additive manufacturing, microfluidics, experimental characterization, computer vision for materials processing.

Tools and Methods

ANSYS Workbench, SolidWorks, Python (OpenCV, NumPy), FDM additive manufacturing (Bambu Lab X1C), optical microscopy, impedance spectroscopy, lean manufacturing methods.
